name: Federal Wildland Firefighter (Seasonal)
operator: USDA Forest Service / DOI (BLM, NPS, FWS, BIA)
summary: Entry-level seasonal firefighting on engine, handcrew, or hotshot crews, hired at the new GW pay grades created by the 2021-2025 federal firefighter pay reforms. Base pay is modest but overtime, hazard pay, incident premium pay, and per diem are where the season's money actually comes from.
other_eligibility: Must pass the arduous Work Capacity Test (3 miles, 45 lb pack, 45 min). Federal background check, drug testing, valid driver's license. Red Card / basic wildland fire training (S-130/S-190/L-180) typically provided at hire. Physically extreme: 14-day rolls, 16-hour shifts, smoke, sleeping on the ground.
pay_note: Base only, Rest-of-US GW table: GW-3 $20.93/hr, GW-4 $22.97/hr, GW-5 $25.12/hr; locality pay adds on top (one source reports GW-4 step 1 at $23.20/hr in a locality area). NOTHING IS DEDUCTED FOR HOUSING WHEN DEPLOYED — on incident assignment, lodging is paid by the government and you collect the $68/day federal per diem for meals and incidentals on top of wages. At your home duty station, government barracks/quarters are sometimes available BUT ARE CHARGED A FEE, and many rookies rent their own place in an expensive fire-town market — this is the one real cost. Overtime is base x 1.5 and is the bulk of earnings; hazard pay adds 25% of base for uncontrolled fireline; Incident Response Premium Pay (new under the 2025 Act) adds a daily supplement of 450% of your hourly base rate, capped at $9,000 per calendar year. Illustrative 16-hour fire day for a GW-4: $185.60 base + $278.40 OT + $92.80 hazard = $556.80.
net_take_home_note: A typical busy 6-month season for an entry GW-3 totals about $53,894 gross including OT, hazard, incident pay and per diem; a busy 3-month student season about $26,947; a big year on a hotshot crew can top $82,358. Entry firefighters commonly log ~700 OT hours in a good season, hotshots 1,000-1,200. Because food and lodging are covered on assignment, a firefighter who is out on rolls most of the summer spends almost nothing and can bank the majority of it.
cost_note: Boots (NFPA-compliant leather lace-ups, $300-$500) are usually the worker's own purchase, plus travel to the duty station and rent/deposit if no barracks. Training is paid.

deadlines.note: Federal fire hiring runs on USAJOBS with the main outreach announcement typically opening in the fall (roughly Sept-Nov) for the following summer, with selections through winter and starts in April-June. Late-season and off-cycle fills continue year-round. Apply in the fall, not the spring.

caveat_note: The headline base rate is not the story in either direction: a slow fire year with little overtime can cut a season's earnings roughly in half, and the $9,000 annual cap on Incident Response Premium Pay bites in a heavy year. Real physical risk, entrapment risk, chronic smoke exposure, and near-total loss of control over your summer schedule. Federal seasonal appointments also make you vulnerable to hiring freezes and shutdown-driven delays.

name: Contract Wildland Fire Crew (Type 2 IA)
operator: Private contractors, e.g. Grayback Forestry, PatRick Environmental (Oregon/Idaho/Montana)
summary: Private companies field Type 2 Initial Attack crews that get dispatched to federal fires under contract, hiring rookies with a much faster and lower-barrier process than USAJOBS. You are paid only when the crew is on assignment, which makes the season more volatile than a federal job.
other_eligibility: Work Capacity Test (arduous pack test), drug testing, valid driver's license typically required. Rookie fire school (usually run by the contractor, sometimes unpaid or partially paid). Must be able to work 14-day rolls of 8-16 hour days.
pay_note: Grayback advertises $17.75 to $28.73/hr plus fringe depending on project and experience; Glassdoor puts Type 2 firefighters around $21-$29/hr. NOTHING DEDUCTED WHILE ON A FIRE — on assignment the contractor covers lodging and food (fire camp), so on-fire days are close to pure savings. The catch is the reverse of a deduction: between dispatches you may be unpaid or on minimal standby hours, and some contractors expect you to house yourself near the shop at your own cost during the season. Overtime after 40 hours is the main earnings driver, same as federal.
net_take_home_note: Highly variable. A rookie on a crew that gets dispatched steadily can approach federal-crew earnings; a crew that sits idle in a wet year earns very little. Ask any contractor directly how many days their crews were dispatched last season before accepting.
cost_note: Boots ($300-$500) plus, at some contractors, the cost of rookie fire school and travel/housing near the shop.

deadlines.note: Contract crews hire on a rolling basis with the bulk of rookie hiring and fire school in Feb-May for a June start; they also backfill mid-season, so a late applicant has a real chance in a way federal hiring does not allow.

caveat_note: Pay-per-dispatch is the whole risk. Contractor crews are called after federal resources in many dispatch orders, so a quiet year can mean a near-zero season. Quality varies enormously between companies — some are professional outfits, some are not. Verify the company's safety record and dispatch history before signing on.

name: CAL FIRE Seasonal Firefighter (Fire Fighter I)
operator: California Department of Forestry and Fire Protection (CAL FIRE)
summary: California's state seasonal firefighter classification, hired in large numbers each year with no prior fire experience required and paid training. It is the standard on-ramp into California municipal and state fire careers, and pays better than most federal entry fire jobs.
other_eligibility: Valid driver's license, physical fitness standard, medical exam, background check and drug screening. No prior firefighting experience required; CAL FIRE runs its own academy. CPR/first aid needed before or during employment.
pay_note: Figures are from salary aggregators (roughly $19-$26/hr, average around $23/hr) rather than a directly verified CAL FIRE pay schedule — treat as approximate. The important structural fact: CAL FIRE seasonals work out of state fire stations and typically SLEEP AND EAT AT THE STATION at no housing cost while on shift, and on extended incidents food and lodging are covered. There is no housing deduction. Extended-attack overtime is where the season's real money is; CAL FIRE seasonals routinely work very long incident hours in a bad California fire year.
net_take_home_note: Not directly sourced. Because station duty removes most living costs during shifts, savings rate is high relative to gross for a worker with no rent at home.
cost_note: Boots and personal gear, plus travel to the assigned unit — CAL FIRE assigns you to a unit anywhere in California, which may be far from home.

deadlines.note: Application cutoffs run November 1-30 with additional cutoffs during the year; hiring begins as early as January and continues as need arises. Applications go through CalCareers; the FFI hotline is 951-901-5051.

caveat_note: Pay figures are aggregator-derived and should be confirmed against the current CalCareers posting before relying on them. California fire seasons are now nearly year-round, so 'seasonal' can mean 9+ months with little control over time off. Physically punishing and genuinely dangerous.

name: National Park Concession Work (Aramark Destinations)
operator: Aramark Destinations — Yosemite Hospitality, Denali, Mesa Verde, Lake Powell, Glen Canyon, Olympic
summary: Front-desk, housekeeping, food service, retail, and recreation jobs inside national parks, with dorm or tent-cabin housing and a meal plan available on site. The housing deduction is very small at most Aramark parks, which is what makes the take-home competitive despite modest hourly rates.
other_eligibility: Background check; drug testing for some roles. Must accept dormitory or canvas-tent living with 2-3 roommates, remote location, limited cell service, and physically repetitive work. Some roles (drivers, guides) require licenses or certifications.
pay_note: Only one wage was directly verified: Seasonal Recreation Worker at Yosemite posted at $19.30/hr. THE DEDUCTIONS ARE THE POINT AND THEY ARE UNUSUALLY LOW. Yosemite: employee rent plus utilities is stated as UNDER $20 PER WEEK for dorm-style housing with 2-3 roommates. Mesa Verde: housing around $50/week. Denali: on-site housing AND a meal plan bundled at $16/DAY ALL INCLUSIVE (about $112/week for both bed and food). Elsewhere Aramark says rates 'vary based on position and type of housing.' Meals are otherwise not free — you get discounts at park food operations and grocery stores and access to community kitchens. Overtime past 40 hours is common in peak season at the busier parks but is not guaranteed and shrinks in shoulder months.
net_take_home_note: At Yosemite, a worker at $19.30/hr for 40 hours grosses about $772/week and loses under $20 to housing — the cheapest rent-to-wage ratio of any employer in this tier. Denali's $16/day bundle costs more but eliminates food spending entirely. Realistic banked savings for a disciplined April-November Yosemite season are substantial because there is almost nothing to spend money on inside the park.
cost_note: Travel to the park (Denali in particular is expensive to reach), plus work-appropriate clothing and gear for a cold or high-elevation site.

deadlines.note: Yosemite recruited for April 1 - November 1 season dates; Denali's ideal dates were May 7 - September 17. Hiring is rolling and opens in winter (roughly Dec-Feb) for the following summer; late applicants are often still placed because turnover is high.

caveat_note: Housing is genuinely rustic — canvas tents and shared cabins with a bed, dresser and bear box. Isolation, limited connectivity, and small-community social friction are the real attrition drivers, not the pay. Wage data beyond the single verified Yosemite posting is unconfirmed; ask for the specific rate in writing before accepting, since roles inside the same park differ by several dollars an hour.

name: National Park Concession Work (Delaware North)
operator: Delaware North — Yellowstone General Stores, Kennedy Space Center, Sequoia, Shenandoah, Grand Canyon
summary: Retail, food service, and lodging jobs run by Delaware North inside Yellowstone and other parks, with dorm housing at a fixed weekly rate and an optional meal plan. The published housing and meal numbers are unusually transparent, which makes the net easy to calculate in advance.
other_eligibility: Background check. Dorm living with roommates or bring-your-own-RV. Remote location with harsh weather and wildlife hazards; long standing shifts.
pay_note: Specific Yellowstone positions posted at $17.20 to $18.20/hr (broader seasonal-Yellowstone aggregate averages a lower $15.86, so entry roles may sit below this band). DEDUCTIONS: dorm-style housing $50/WEEK with free laundry; the optional full meal plan is an ADDITIONAL $75/WEEK. If you take both, $125/week comes out of your check — roughly $3.13/hr off a 40-hour week, i.e. an $18.20 headline job nets about $15.07/hr equivalent. Taking housing only ($50/wk) and cooking or using the 50% shift-meal discount is materially cheaper. RV site with hookups is also $50/week but with coin laundry and communal facilities. Overtime is available in peak summer but not guaranteed.
net_take_home_note: At $18.20/hr, 40 hrs/week: $728 gross, minus $50 housing = $678 before tax if you skip the meal plan, or $603 with it. Over a 16-week core season that is roughly $10,800 vs $9,650 gross-after-deduction — the meal plan costs about $1,200 across a season, so it only pays if it genuinely replaces all your food spending.
cost_note: Travel to Yellowstone (nearest airports are Bozeman, Jackson, Cody — all expensive), cold-weather clothing, and non-slip work shoes.

deadlines.note: Yellowstone concession hiring opens in winter (roughly Nov-Feb) for a May-October season and continues rolling; mid-season backfill hiring in June-July is common because of high early attrition.

caveat_note: Many concessioners pay an end-of-season completion bonus that is forfeited entirely if you leave early — verify the amount and the exact terms before counting on it, and understand that it converts a bad-fit situation into an expensive one. Hours can be cut in shoulder season while the weekly housing charge stays fixed, which is the scenario where the deduction hurts most.

name: Residential Summer Camp Counselor
operator: ACA-accredited overnight camps (independent, YMCA, Scouting, nonprofit)
summary: Live-in counselor at an overnight children's camp for an 8-10 week summer, paid a flat seasonal salary with room, board and laundry fully covered. Cash pay is low but the deduction is zero, so the savings rate is close to 100%.
other_eligibility: Most ACA camps require you to be 18 and a high school graduate before the season starts. Criminal background check and sex-offender registry check are standard and non-negotiable. Lifeguard, WFA/WFR, ropes-course, or activity-specific certifications raise pay and are sometimes reimbursed. You live with campers, are on duty most waking hours, and get roughly one day off per week.
pay_note: Typical first-year residential counselor pay works out to roughly $325-$500 per week of the contract, usually quoted as a flat season salary rather than an hourly rate; specialists (waterfront director, head of kayaking, riding, climbing) and returning staff earn more. NOTHING IS DEDUCTED — room, all meals, and usually laundry are provided free and are not charged back. That is the entire financial argument for this job: the low headline number is also the net number. Beware that the flat salary divided by actual hours worked is often below minimum wage on paper; camps operate under a specific FLSA seasonal-establishment exemption, so do not expect overtime. Aggregator 'camp counselor' salary figures above $30k/yr are contaminated by year-round camp administrator roles and should be ignored.
net_take_home_note: A 9-week season at $400/week is about $3,600 gross with essentially zero living expenses for those 9 weeks — comparable in real savings terms to a much higher-paying job where you pay rent. It will not fund a year off, but it costs nothing to do.
cost_note: Travel to camp (some camps reimburse partially), plus certification costs if not reimbursed — lifeguard certification runs roughly $200-$400, Wilderness First Aid $200-$300.

deadlines.note: Camp hiring runs roughly November through April for a mid-June start, with the strongest camps filling by February and stragglers hiring into May. The ACA job board (jobs.acacamps.org) and CampChannel are the main aggregators.

caveat_note: This is the lowest-cash option in this tier by a wide margin. The trade is real responsibility for children, near-total loss of privacy and free time for two months, and pay that only makes sense because your expenses go to zero. Verify whether the quoted number is for the full contract or per week — camps state it both ways and the difference is enormous.

name: Cruise Ship Entry-Level Crew (Foreign-Flag Lines)
operator: Royal Caribbean, Carnival, NCL and similar foreign-flagged operators
summary: Entry-level shipboard hospitality on the large international cruise lines, with free cabin and meals for the duration of a contract. In practice the low-skill roles are effectively closed to American applicants, and Americans are hired mainly into specialist customer-facing positions.
other_eligibility: Seafarer medical exam, STCW basic safety training, C1/D transit visa for non-US-flag vessels calling at US ports, background check. Contracts of 6-9 months with no days off — crew work 7 days a week for the whole contract.
pay_note: No reliable entry-level figure could be confirmed; US-based aggregator numbers around $16-$22/hr for 'Royal Caribbean' reflect shoreside American jobs, not shipboard crew, and should not be used. Shipboard reality: cabin and all meals are FREE and nothing is deducted for them, but base wages on foreign-flagged vessels are set well below US norms because the ships are registered in Panama, the Bahamas or Liberia specifically to avoid US wage and labor law. Tipped positions live on gratuity pools; non-tipped positions do not.
net_take_home_note: Not sourceable at entry level with confidence.
cost_note: STCW basic safety training (roughly $800-$1,200), seafarer medical, visa fees, and flights to the join port if not reimbursed.

deadlines.note: Hiring is continuous through licensed crewing agencies rather than seasonal; expect 2-6 months from application to join date.

exclude_reason: Effectively not open to American entry-level applicants. Low-skill shipboard roles — galley, housekeeping, bedroom stewards, janitorial — are filled almost exclusively from Indonesia, the Philippines and similar labor markets at wage levels US applicants will not accept. Americans are hired into specialist roles (casino dealers, performers, fitness instructors, shore excursion and cruise staff, retail) that require prior credentials, not into the entry tier this directory is describing. Listed for completeness and to warn readers off, not as a viable gap-year on-ramp.
caveat_note: Beware any 'cruise ship job placement' service charging a fee — legitimate lines and their crewing agents do not charge applicants. The realistic American path is the US-flag small-ship operators instead.

name: US-Flag Small Ship Crew (Deckhand / Steward)
operator: American Cruise Lines and comparable US-flagged domestic operators
summary: Entry deck and hotel crew on US-flagged riverboats and small coastal ships, which by law must be crewed by Americans — making this the version of cruise work that is actually open to US young adults. Pay is quoted as a flat weekly rate with cabin and meals free for a roughly 28-week contract.
other_eligibility: TWIC card and often a Merchant Mariner Credential (MMC) for deck roles; drug testing under USCG rules, physical, background check. You live aboard for the whole contract and work 7 days a week with no days off in port.
pay_note: Postings advertise $1,000-$1,400 per week plus bonuses. CABIN AND ALL MEALS ARE FREE AND NOTHING IS DEDUCTED — this is a genuine zero-expense job. The catch is buried in the hourly math: employee-reported average hourly pay is about $13.34, which means that $1,000-$1,400 weekly is being spread across roughly 75-100 hours of work per week, seven days a week. Judge it as a total-savings number, not as a wage. Reported median total pay is about $40,624/yr for deckhands and $34,799/yr for stewards, consistent with long contracts at those weekly rates.
net_take_home_note: A full 28-week contract at $1,100/week is roughly $30,800 gross with effectively zero living costs for those seven months — one of the highest genuinely-bankable totals in this entire tier for someone with no credentials.
cost_note: TWIC card (about $125-$200), MMC application and medical if required, and travel to the join port.

deadlines.note: Hires continuously year-round across river and coastal itineraries; heaviest recruiting ahead of the spring season start.

caveat_note: The seven-days-a-week, no-days-off structure over 28 weeks is the real cost and drives high attrition — the effective hourly rate is low and there is nowhere to go at the end of a shift. Confirm before signing whether any bonus is contingent on completing the full contract, since walking away early can forfeit a large chunk of the total.

name: Dude Ranch Wrangler / Guest Ranch Staff
operator: Independent guest ranches (Dude Ranchers' Association members) across WY, MT, CO, AZ
summary: Horseback wrangling, housekeeping, kitchen and guest-service roles at Western guest ranches, with room and board included and guest gratuities on top. Tips are a meaningful share of total pay and are rarely reflected in the advertised rate.
other_eligibility: Valid driver's license commonly required. Wrangler roles need real horsemanship, and some ranches set the wrangler minimum age at 21 or even 25 for insurance reasons — non-wrangler roles (housekeeping, kitchen, kids' program) have no such bar. Long six-day weeks, early mornings, outdoor physical work.
pay_note: Verified postings: Rancho de los Caballeros (AZ) wrangler at $16.00/hr plus gratuities when guests are in house; another listing at $18.00/hr plus room, board and tips. DEDUCTIONS ARE SMALL BUT NOT ALWAYS ZERO — Rancho de los Caballeros charges an $80 HOUSING FEE PER PAY PERIOD (roughly $40/week), while UXU Ranch and Red Rock Ranch include room and board with no stated charge and Red Rock provides a shared room and bathroom with one other employee. Always ask whether room and board is free or a payroll deduction, because both models are common in this sector and neither is stated in the headline. Gratuities are pooled at most ranches and can add materially to a season, but they are guest-dependent and unguaranteed.
net_take_home_note: At $16-$18/hr with free or near-free room and board plus pooled tips, a full June-September season is comparable to a park concession job, with the tips being the swing factor. A ranch charging $80/pay period still nets far better than any market rent.
cost_note: Travel to remote Western locations, plus boots, jeans and a hat for wrangler roles (some ranches offer a clothing discount rather than an allowance).

deadlines.note: Guest ranch seasons run roughly June 1 to mid-September (UXU: June 1 - September 15; Red Rock: spring through August 22). Hiring peaks January-April; ranches also post urgent mid-season openings on CoolWorks and RanchWork.com in June-July.

caveat_note: Wrangler roles often carry an age floor of 21-25, so an 18-year-old should target housekeeping, kitchen or kids' program roles instead and expect lower tips. These are small family businesses with wide variation in professionalism, hours tracking, and how honestly the tip pool is split — talk to a returning employee before committing.

name: Alaska Fishing Lodge Crew
operator: Remote Alaskan sportfishing lodges (e.g. Whalers Cove, Kingfisher Charters, Wilderness Place Lodge)
summary: Housekeeping, serving, dock and fish-processing crew at fly-in or boat-in sportfishing lodges from May to September, with a private room and three guest-menu meals a day included. Guest tips and an end-of-season bonus are a large and highly variable part of total pay.
other_eligibility: Background check; some lodges require food handler cards or drug testing. Extremely remote — often no road access, limited internet, no days off during guest weeks. Physically demanding wet outdoor work for dock and fillet crew.
pay_note: No lodge publishes hard wage figures — Whalers Cove states only 'daily rate' for guides and 'commensurate with experience' for senior roles, and aggregator weekly figures for 'Alaska fishing room and board jobs' ($1,663-$2,442/week) are contaminated by captain, guide and chef roles and should not be applied to entry positions. WHAT IS CONFIRMED AND MATTERS: room and board are provided as a benefit, not a deduction — a private room plus three meals a day on the same menu as paying guests, with typical schedules of 7-9 hour shifts and 40-50+ hours a week including overtime, plus tips and a seasonal bonus. Some lodges add a tiered travel benefit earned by returning seasons. Nothing comes out of the check for housing or food.
net_take_home_note: Not reliably sourceable at entry level. The structural advantage is that a 14-18 week season in a place with literally nowhere to spend money converts nearly all gross pay into savings.
cost_note: Airfare to Alaska and often a float plane or ferry connection to the lodge, sometimes reimbursed only on completing the season. Rain gear and boots.

deadlines.note: Staff arrive May through mid-June and depart in September; guest season runs roughly the third week of June to the first week of September. Lodges post for the following summer starting in the fall and hire through the winter, with most positions gone by March.

caveat_note: Get the wage, the tip policy, the bonus amount and the travel reimbursement terms in writing before flying to Alaska — vague 'commensurate with experience' language is the norm in this sector and leaves you with no leverage once you are somewhere you cannot leave without a plane. Travel reimbursement is frequently contingent on finishing the season.

name: Whitewater Raft Guide
operator: Independent outfitters (e.g. Nantahala Outdoor Center, Colorado and West Virginia outfitters)
summary: Guiding commercial rafting trips after completing an outfitter's guide school, paid per trip or hourly with tips forming a large share of income. It is one of the few jobs in this tier where the worker pays upfront before earning anything.
other_eligibility: Must complete guide school and pass a check-out run: typically 50-100 hours of on-river training over 4-5 weeks. Swiftwater rescue and CPR/first aid or Wilderness First Responder are usually required. Strong swimmer, physically demanding, real drowning risk.
pay_note: First-year guides commonly start around $15.00/hr plus gratuity; national averages sit near $16.16/hr, and established operations like the US National Whitewater Center average about $22/hr. Per-trip structures are also common: new guides typically make $50-$100 per day plus tips, experienced guides $150-$200 plus tips. TIPS ARE NOT A ROUNDING ERROR — a first-year guide working a full season can add $1,500 or more in gratuities. HOUSING VARIES SHARPLY AND IS THE THING TO ASK ABOUT: many outfitters offer free or nearly free staff camping/bunkhouse on company land, some charge a weekly rate, and some offer nothing in an expensive river town. Meals are generally not provided outside guide school. Water levels drive the schedule — low-water weeks mean cancelled trips and no pay.
net_take_home_note: Modest. A summer of guiding rarely nets more than a few thousand dollars after the guide school cost, and the honest framing is that people do it for the life rather than the money.
cost_note: Guide school is a real upfront cost: NOC's starts at $300 including instruction, gear, daily meals and basecamp lodging; other schools run about $850. Some outfitters take a $300 deposit that is REFUNDED if you are hired and work through the season's end (one program specified through August 15). Add swiftwater rescue and WFR certification if not bundled.

deadlines.note: Guide schools run in March-May for a Memorial Day through Labor Day season; register in winter (Jan-March) since schools fill and completing one is a prerequisite for being hired.

caveat_note: You pay to train and completing guide school does not guarantee a job — outfitters check out more candidates than they hire. Income is weather- and water-dependent, so a drought summer can gut the season. Confirm the refund terms on any deposit and whether staff housing is free, charged, or nonexistent before paying for a school.

name: Antarctic Support Contractor (McMurdo / South Pole / Palmer)
operator: KBR Mission Technology Solutions (prime contractor since June 2, 2026, replacing Leidos) and subcontractors including Gana-A'Yoo Services Corporation
summary: Entry-level support roles — dining attendant, janitorial steward, general assistant — on the US Antarctic Program's austral summer deployment, roughly October to January. Housing, all meals, and travel from the US gateway are fully covered, so the paycheck is almost entirely savings.
other_eligibility: US citizenship is required by the contract. Must obtain a Public Trust security clearance before start, and must pass the NSF's demanding Physical Qualification (PQ) process including full physical and DENTAL examinations — the dental exam disqualifies a meaningful number of applicants. Drug testing, background check. You cannot leave the continent mid-deployment.
pay_note: Verified 2026-2027 season postings through subcontractor Gana-A'Yoo: Lead Janitor at McMurdo $648-$736 per week, Steward Coordinator (janitorial) $729-$829 per week. Non-lead entry roles (dining attendant, janitorial steward, general assistant) pay below this band. EVERYTHING IS COVERED AND NOTHING IS DEDUCTED — dorm berthing, all meals in the galley, laundry, and round-trip travel from the US gateway city (usually Christchurch, NZ) are provided by the contractor at no cost to the worker. There is essentially nothing to spend money on at McMurdo beyond the store and the bars. Long weeks (typically 54 hours, six days) with overtime included in the structure.
net_take_home_note: A full October-January austral summer deployment of about 14 weeks at roughly $700/week is around $9,800 gross with zero living costs and zero travel costs — close to a 100% savings rate, which is the highest of any option in this tier.
cost_note: The real cost is the PQ medical and dental workup, which you may pay for out of pocket if uninsured, plus any dental work needed to pass. Extreme cold-weather gear is issued.

deadlines.note: Deployment runs roughly October to January (2026-2027 postings specified October 2026 to January 2027). Hiring and PQ processing start very early — postings typically go up in the northern spring and summer (roughly April-August) for an October deployment, because clearance and medical qualification take months. Watch usap.gov/jobsandopportunities and KBR's careers site.

caveat_note: VERIFY THE EMPLOYER NAME BEFORE APPLYING — the prime contract changed hands on June 2, 2026 from Leidos to KBR under a new 20-year, $8 billion Antarctic Science and Engineering Support Contract, so older guides and job boards still point at Leidos. Expect transition-year disruption in hiring processes. The PQ medical/dental gate is the most common reason applicants are dropped, often late in the process after they have already turned down other work. Once deployed you cannot leave, and the social environment is intense and confined.

name: Alaska Commercial Fishing Deckhand
operator: Independent vessel owners (salmon seine, gillnet, longline, troll); placement help via ALFA and BBRSDA
summary: Crewing on a small independent fishing vessel for a salmon or longline season, paid a percentage of the boat's catch rather than a wage. It is the highest-variance option in this tier: a good boat in a good run pays exceptionally well and a bad one pays almost nothing.
other_eligibility: Alaska commercial crew license required (inexpensive, bought online). No experience formally required but green crew are hired last. Extremely physically demanding, sleep-deprived, and genuinely dangerous — commercial fishing has one of the highest occupational fatality rates in the US. Drug-free expectation set by the skipper, not a formal program.
pay_note: THERE IS NO WAGE — you are paid a 'crew share,' typically 1-10% of the net value of the boat's harvest, and you are not paid until the end of the season. The structure: the skipper takes roughly 35-40%, then FUEL, FOOD, BAIT AND OTHER BOAT EXPENSES ARE DEDUCTED OFF THE TOP before the remainder is split among crew. This is the deduction that matters and it is invisible in any recruiting pitch. Worked example: a five-man purse seiner catching $200,000 of salmon gives each deckhand a 10% share of about $20,000, less about $3,000 in expenses, leaving roughly $17,000 for the summer. Bunk and food aboard are covered but the food is charged back against the boat's expenses before your share is calculated — it is not free, it is deducted collectively.
net_take_home_note: The sourced example nets about $17,000 for a summer season on a productive seiner. That same berth on a boat that misses the run can net close to zero, and there is no floor.
cost_note: Airfare to Alaska plus several weeks of living costs in a fishing town while looking for a berth if you go up without a pre-arranged job. Raingear, boots, gloves and a sleeping bag. Alaska crew license fee.

deadlines.note: Bristol Bay salmon runs late June to late July; Southeast troll and longline seasons are longer. Berths are arranged from roughly January through May; ALFA runs a crew training and placement program that places deckhands mostly on troll and longline vessels with some seine and gillnet berths. Showing up in Naknek or Sitka in June to walk the docks still works but is a gamble.

caveat_note: No fish, no money — this is the purest version of that risk in the whole directory, and unlike processing work there is no hourly floor to fall back on. Verify the crew share percentage AND which expenses come off the top BEFORE stepping aboard, and get it in writing; disputes over shares are common and you have little recourse from a boat in Bristol Bay. Real fatality and serious-injury risk. Note this is distinct from Alaska seafood PROCESSING, which pays hourly.

name: Reforestation Tree Planting (US)
operator: Private silviculture contractors in the Pacific Northwest; some agency/conservation-corps hourly crews
summary: Planting seedlings on logged or burned ground, paid either hourly by agency and conservation employers or by the tree on private contract crews. The famous high-earning version of this job is Canadian and is not open to Americans without a work permit.
other_eligibility: Drug testing common on contract crews. Brutally physical: steep burned or slash-covered ground, 8-10 hour days in cold spring rain, heavy bags of seedlings. Reliable transport to remote units; crews often camp or motel out.
pay_note: Two pay models. HOURLY ($15-$22/hr) is typical of government and conservation employers and is what a beginner should target — most beginners earn more hourly than on piece rate. PIECE RATE runs roughly $0.10-$0.30 per tree; experienced planters putting in 1,500-2,500 trees a day earn substantially more, but a first-week rookie planting a few hundred trees a day can fall below minimum wage before make-up pay. Housing and meals are usually NOT provided by US contractors — crews commonly share motel rooms or camp at their own cost, and that lodging cost is the deduction to budget for. Some contractors deduct transport or lodging from pay; confirm which.
net_take_home_note: Not reliably sourceable. Because lodging is generally self-funded and unlike park or lodge work there is no free bed, net is meaningfully below gross.
cost_note: Caulk boots, rain gear, planting bags and shovel (sometimes supplied), plus shared lodging or camping costs and travel between units.

deadlines.note: The US planting season is late winter to spring — roughly January through May in the Pacific Northwest, not summer. Hire in the fall and early winter for a late-winter start. This does NOT stack with a summer job the way most entries here do; it stacks with a summer fire or park season.

caveat_note: the lucrative tree-planting culture young people have heard about is CANADIAN and requires a Canadian work permit that Americans do not automatically get. In the US, roughly 85% of the 1.5 billion trees planted annually are put in the ground by H-2B guest workers on contractor crews, so the pipeline into private US planting crews is built around visa labor rather than domestic seasonal hires. Americans realistically access this work through agency, conservation corps, or hourly crews rather than the high-earning piece-rate contract crews. Wrong season for a classic summer earning block, physically the hardest entry on this list, and the domestic hiring pipeline is thin. Anyone drawn here by Canadian tree-planting stories should be told plainly that they cannot simply go do that.

name: Seasonal Agricultural Harvest Work
operator: Fruit and vegetable growers, primarily Washington, Oregon, California, Michigan
summary: Picking and packing apples, cherries, berries and similar crops during a short intense harvest window, usually paid piece rate against an hourly minimum. Domestic workers are legally treated differently from H-2A guest workers on both wages and housing, in ways that cut both directions.
other_eligibility: Generally no background check or certification. Physically demanding: ladders, heavy picking bags, extreme heat, repetitive strain. Own transport usually needed to reach orchards.
pay_note: Washington's 2026 Adverse Effect Wage Rate is $16.53/hr for entry-level farmworkers and $19.00/hr for skilled positions, down sharply from the $19.82 AEWR at the start of 2025 under new rules. TWO DEDUCTION FACTS THAT MATTER AND CUT OPPOSITE WAYS: (1) employers may deduct housing costs ONLY from H-2A guest workers, NOT from corresponding domestic workers, even when a domestic worker lives in the same employer-provided housing — so a US worker in grower housing may pay nothing for it while the H-2A worker beside them loses about $2.49/hr in Washington. (2) But domestic workers in eight states including Washington move to the STATE MINIMUM WAGE rather than the higher AEWR as of January 1, 2026, so the domestic worker's floor is lower. Piece rate is the norm at harvest with the applicable minimum as a make-up floor; a fast experienced picker beats the hourly rate substantially and a first-week rookie does not.
net_take_home_note: Not reliably sourceable, and highly dependent on picking speed. Grower housing where available and free is the main lever on net; otherwise harvest-town rents in short supply during the season eat a large share.
cost_note: Transport to and around the growing region, and housing if grower housing is unavailable — which is the common case for domestic hires, since most grower housing is built for the H-2A program.

deadlines.note: Harvest windows are short and crop-specific: Washington cherries roughly June-July, apples roughly late August through October. Hiring is walk-up and rolling right before and during the window, not months ahead. Postings appear on seasonaljobs.dol.gov, where the H-2B/H-2A clearance orders state the exact wage and any housing terms.

caveat_note: The clearance-order wage on seasonaljobs.dol.gov is the most reliable single source for what any given farm actually pays — read it before you go. Short harvest windows mean you cannot build a full season out of one crop, and weather can delay or compress the window with no compensation. This is physically punishing work in a labor market largely structured around guest workers rather than domestic seasonal hires.

name: Remote Camp Support (Alaska / North Slope)
operator: NANA Management Services (NMS) and comparable Alaska Native corporation camp-services contractors
summary: Housekeeping, janitorial, kitchen and camp-attendant work at remote oilfield, mining and industrial camps, typically on a three-weeks-on, three-weeks-off rotation with twelve-hour days. Housing, all meals and flights to camp are covered, so the entire rotation is worked at zero personal expense.
other_eligibility: Pre-employment drug testing and physical assessment are strict and non-negotiable in this industry, including random testing on site. Many postings ask for about one year of prior commercial housekeeping experience, which is the main barrier for a true first-timer. Must be able to live in dormitory-style camp conditions. Alaska Native corporation hiring preference may apply.
pay_note: Most North Slope camp postings say 'Wage DOE' without a published rate; a Nome-based remote janitor posting listed $15/hr and up DOE, and a hospital housekeeper role in the same company was posted at $27/hr, so the band is wide and location-dependent. THE STRUCTURE IS THE VALUE, NOT THE RATE: 3-weeks-on / 3-weeks-off rotation at TWELVE HOURS PER DAY, seven days a week on shift, with HOUSING AND ALL MEALS PROVIDED FREE and camp flights covered. Twelve-hour days seven days a week means roughly 84 hours per week, so overtime past 40 is guaranteed and structural rather than occasional — the effective weekly gross at even a modest base rate is far above what the hourly number suggests. Nothing is deducted for room or board.
net_take_home_note: Not directly sourced, but the arithmetic is favorable: a 3-week rotation of 84-hour weeks with 44 of those hours at time-and-a-half, at zero living cost, banks more per rotation than most full-time entry jobs bank in two months. The off-rotation weeks are unpaid, which is the offsetting factor.
cost_note: Travel to the Alaska gateway city (usually Anchorage) at your own cost; the camp flight itself is covered. Work boots and cold-weather clothing.

deadlines.note: Camp support hires continuously year-round rather than seasonally, with heavier demand around North Slope winter construction season. Postings appear on nmsusa.com careers and the major job boards.

caveat_note: Published wages are rare — the 'Wage DOE' convention means you will not know what you are being paid until an offer, so ask for the rate and the OT structure explicitly. The prior-experience requirement screens out many first-time workers. Twelve-hour days for 21 consecutive days in a dry camp with no privacy is genuinely hard, and the off-rotation weeks are unpaid, so annualized income is lower than the on-rotation math implies.

name: Traveling Carnival / Fair Worker
operator: Butler Amusements, Reithoffer Shows and similar traveling carnival companies
summary: Setting up, operating and tearing down rides and games as a carnival moves between county fairs and festivals across a long season. Bunkhouse lodging travels with the show, but the pay is the lowest of any option in this tier.
other_eligibility: Generally minimal screening. Heavy manual labor on setup and teardown, frequent overnight moves between towns, working outdoors in all weather, and long stretches with no days off during a fair run.
pay_note: Figures from an actual DOL seasonal clearance order for a traveling carnival Amusement & Recreation Attendant: $11.59-$15.11/hr, 40 hours per week, 1:00 PM - 10:00 PM, with the posting explicitly stating NO OVERTIME EXPECTED — which removes the single biggest earnings lever available in every other job in this tier. Bunkhouse lodging travels with the show and is commonly advertised as free, but bunkhouse quality and whether any charge applies vary by company and are frequently not stated in postings. Meals are not provided. Aggregator figures around $21/hr for 'traveling carnival' are contaminated by management and specialty roles; carnival ride workers typically earn $10-$15/hr.
net_take_home_note: At roughly $13/hr with no overtime, 40 hours is about $520/week gross. Even with free bunkhouse lodging, this is the weakest net in this tier by a clear margin — nearly every other entry here beats it once deductions are counted.
cost_note: Getting to the show's first stop, plus all food, since meals are not provided.

deadlines.note: The verified clearance order ran January 9 to November 8 — a nine to ten month route, far longer than a summer. Hiring is rolling and largely walk-up; postings appear on seasonaljobs.dol.gov and company employment pages. Much of this workforce is H-2B, so domestic hiring is opportunistic.

caveat_note: Low pay, no overtime, and a nine-month route make this a poor financial choice compared with the rest of this tier — include it for completeness, not as a recommendation. Bunkhouse life means zero privacy for months. Verify in writing whether lodging is actually free and whether anything is deducted, since the DOL posting was silent on both.

name: Seasonal Ski Patroller
summary: Winter-season patrolling — medical response, hazard marking, avalanche mitigation — at a ski area, requiring EMT or Outdoor Emergency Care certification obtained before you are hired. It pays noticeably better than other resort-season roles but has a real credential barrier.
other_eligibility: EMT-B or NSP Outdoor Emergency Care (OEC) certification is required, plus expert-level skiing or riding ability tested on hire. Avalanche education (Avy 1 at minimum) is expected at resorts with avalanche terrain, and prior patrol or mitigation experience gets priority. Early morning starts, work in storms, real avalanche and trauma exposure.
pay_note: Aggregator data puts US ski patrol around $20.46/hr average with most between $20.19 and $21.88; EMT-designated patrol roles average about $20.78 with a wider $16.35-$22.12 band — treat as approximate rather than verified employer figures. THE DEDUCTION QUESTION IS THE WHOLE STORY IN SKI TOWNS. Where an employer offers subsidized staff housing it is typically deducted from pay at a fixed rate; where it does not, market rent in Colorado, Utah and Wyoming resort towns will consume most of a patroller's wage, and a $22/hr job with no housing nets far less than an $18/hr job with a bed included. A season pass is included everywhere and is a genuine several-thousand-dollar in-kind benefit. Overtime exists on storm days but the season is short.
net_take_home_note: Not reliably sourceable and entirely dependent on whether the resort provides housing. Ask for the housing deduction figure before comparing two offers on hourly rate.
cost_note: The certification is a real upfront cost paid before employment: EMT-B courses commonly run $1,000-$2,000 and NSP OEC courses several hundred dollars, plus avalanche coursework. Skis, boots and gear are usually your own.

deadlines.note: Patrol hiring runs roughly August through October for a late-November start, earlier than general resort hiring because certifications must be verified. Because OEC and EMT courses take a full semester, a candidate needs to start the certification about a year before the season they want to work.

caveat_note: This is not a walk-up job — the certification requirement means you must plan roughly a year ahead and spend real money before earning anything, which makes it a poor fit for someone deciding in August what to do this winter. Wage figures here are aggregator-derived. Short season plus expensive resort-town housing is the classic trap where a good-looking hourly rate nets very little.

name: National Park Service Seasonal (via USAJOBS)
operator: National Park Service, US Department of the Interior
summary: Federal seasonal appointments as interpretive rangers, visitor use assistants, trail crew, fee collectors and maintenance staff, hired through USAJOBS on a fixed October-to-February application cycle. Park housing is often available but is rented, not free — unlike the concessioner jobs in the same parks.
other_eligibility: Federal background investigation, drug testing for some positions, valid driver's license. Interpretive rangers may be REQUIRED to live in government quarters, wear a uniform, be available on-call including weekends and holidays, and work overtime. Some roles require prior public-speaking, trail, or law enforcement training.
pay_note: Band shown is GS-5 base for 2026 ($34,799 to $45,239 annually, roughly $16.67-$21.68/hr), before locality pay which adds meaningfully in most park locations. Entry seasonals are frequently hired at GS-3 or GS-4 and earn less than this band; GS-5 typically requires relevant coursework or experience. THE CRITICAL DEDUCTION: ALL NPS EMPLOYEES LIVING IN PARK HOUSING PAY RENT AND UTILITIES, commonly by automatic payroll deduction, and the rate is set by a market-comparability formula rather than being a nominal fee like the concessioners charge. This is the single biggest difference between an NPS seasonal job and an Aramark or Delaware North job in the same park — the concessioner may charge under $20 a week while the government charges something closer to real rent. Some parks have no housing at all, leaving you to find a room in a gateway town. Meals are never provided. Overtime is available in peak season for some roles.
net_take_home_note: Not directly sourceable — depends entirely on the park's quarters rent, which varies by unit and must be asked about specifically. A GS-4/5 seasonal paying real quarters rent can net less than a concessioner employee earning a lower hourly wage in the same park.
cost_note: Travel to the park and a rent deposit; uniforms are typically provided or allowanced for interpretive roles.

deadlines.note: The NPS generally accepts applications for summer positions between OCTOBER AND FEBRUARY for seasons running March through September — miss that window and there is no second chance for the summer. Search 'National Park Service' on USAJOBS and filter Work Type to Temporary. Up to 1,560 NPS seasonal positions in 2026 were nine-month appointments with the remainder mostly six-month.

caveat_note: Federal hiring is slow, rigid, and vulnerable to freezes, budget fights and shutdown-driven delays — recent years have seen NPS seasonal hiring paused, cut and restored on short notice, so treat an offer as uncertain until you have a firm start date. The USAJOBS resume format is unforgiving and most rejections are formatting failures rather than merit ones. Financially this is usually worse than concessioner work in the same park because the government charges real rent; the reason to do it is the federal service credit and the ranger experience, not the money.
